overview: This 693-page file documents the intense 1938 controversy over American economic support for Japan during the Sino-Japanese War. Its 307 documents combine mass petitions, church resolutions, citizen and congressional correspondence, eyewitness accounts of atrocities and aerial bombing, diplomatic and military intelligence, trade statistics, and internal memoranda concerning exports of aircraft, arms, oil, scrap iron, cotton, trucks, machinery, credit, and other strategic resources. Across the file, religious organizations, peace activists, missionaries, labor groups, and private citizens press the Roosevelt administration to impose an embargo, while the State Department repeatedly argues that the Neutrality Act had not been invoked, would apply to both China and Japan, and did not authorize restrictions on most raw materials. Intelligence reports on Japanese procurement, foreign arms suppliers, and the expansion of Japan’s armaments industry place this domestic debate within the wider material economy of the war.
interest: The file is especially valuable for showing how ordinary Americans—particularly Methodists and other church-based activists—connected trade policy to moral responsibility for atrocities in China. Its juxtaposition of petitions with highly repetitive official replies exposes the gap between popular demands for economic sanctions and the administration’s legalistic defense of restraint. Diplomatic and intelligence reports on trucks, aircraft, metals, credit, foreign suppliers, and industrial conversion also allow historians to reconstruct the material foundations of Japan’s war effort. The extensive signature rolls, export figures, and internal tracking of embargo demands make the file useful for studying organized public opinion as well as policymaking.
